title: The daemon gets its first durable recurring schedule, restart-safe and never doubled
description:
SPIDR grandchild A of task-6ec875f4dd5f4f2ab97e46f71bf57b2b (architect-aa54e231, 2026-09-05), split because the parent needed the daemon's FIRST recurring loop plus a probe, a bounded ring, a derived state and an incident - five pieces over twelve-plus files. This row is the dependency-free LEAF and it is pure infrastructure. Grandchild B consumes it.

THE DAEMON HAS NO RECURRING LOOP AT ALL. Measured at HEAD (branch moe/work-2026-09-04): `grep -rn "setInterval" apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts` excluding tests returns ZERO, and daemon-main.ts has no periodic tick. Everything the daemon does today is request-driven or spawn-driven. So this row is not "add a timer to the existing scheduler" - it is the first scheduled work in the process, and that is exactly why the parent's DoD 3 hazard exists.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: a durable recurring schedule. Registered targets with a per-target interval, persisted so a restart resumes them, and an IDEMPOTENT registration so a restart cannot end up running the same target twice.

THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE IS THE SUBJECT. A restart that re-registers an already-scheduled target doubles the rate SILENTLY - the symptom is a durable store filling twice as fast, never an error, and nobody looks until the store is large. Assert the RATE across a restart, not merely that work resumed. A test that only checks "it is still scheduled" passes for a doubled schedule.

BUILD IT INJECTABLE. Take the clock and the timer as ports the way `verifier-process-runner.ts` takes `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs` and `killProcessGroup` (options at :45-56) - a scheduler tested against a real wall clock is slow and flaky, and this repo already has a spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests (~10 s stalls). Every arm here must run on a fake clock in milliseconds.

STOP CLEANLY. Timers keep a node process alive; a schedule with no shutdown path makes the daemon unkillable and makes every test that starts one leak a handle. Copy `verifier-process-runner.ts`'s discipline: one cleanup, called on every exit path, idempotent (:107-118).

NOT IN SCOPE: the health probe itself, the probe ring, UP/DEGRADED/DOWN, and the incident - all grandchild B. No UI.

VERIFY: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`.
definitionOfDone: A target registered with an interval runs on that interval, asserted on an INJECTED clock and timer rather than a real one - no arm in this row may depend on wall-clock time, because the measured spawn-latency cliff on this host reds timing-sensitive tests for unrelated reasons.

REGISTRATION IS IDEMPOTENT: registering the same target twice leaves ONE schedule, asserted by counting executions over a fixed window rather than by inspecting a registry. A registry-count assertion passes for a design that stores one entry and arms two timers.

SURVIVES A RESTART WITH NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE: rebuild the scheduler from durable records and assert the post-restart execution RATE equals the pre-restart rate over the same window. Asserting that work merely resumed is what lets a silently doubled schedule ship - and its only symptom is a store filling twice as fast.

EVERY TIMER IS RELEASED ON SHUTDOWN, asserted by the process being able to exit (or by an explicit handle count), not by a flag. A leaked interval keeps node alive and makes any test that starts a schedule leak into its neighbours.
The per-target interval is durable and a target with no interval takes a stated default; assert the default is applied rather than the target being skipped.
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`.
taskRails: NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE, AND ASSERT THE RATE. 'It resumed after restart' is the assertion that lets a doubled schedule through; only counting executions over a window catches it.
INJECTED CLOCK AND TIMER ONLY. No arm may wait on real time: this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests for reasons unrelated to the code.
ONE CLEANUP, ON EVERY EXIT PATH, IDEMPOTENT - copy verifier-process-runner.ts:107-118. A leaked interval keeps the process alive and contaminates neighbouring tests.
THIS IS THE DAEMON'S FIRST SCHEDULED WORK. Keep it generic and free of health-probe vocabulary: grandchild B is its first consumer, not its owner.
NO PROBE, NO RING, NO INCIDENT, NO UI - grandchild B and the parent's children 2 and 3.

implementationPlan.description: RED TESTS FIRST, ALL ON A FAKE CLOCK, in the new module's name-matched sibling. Rail 2 is absolute: no arm may wait on wall-clock time — this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff (~10s stalls) that reds timing-sensitive tests for unrelated reasons, making failures unattributable. Inject BOTH the clock and the timer; the test drives time forward explicitly and counts executions; nothing sleeps. Write these and watch them fail: (1) INTERVAL HONOURED (DoD 1) — a target at interval N executes once per N of injected time; advance a known window and assert the EXACT execution count, not "at least once". (2) REGISTRATION IDEMPOTENT (DoD 2) — register the SAME target twice, advance a fixed window, assert the count equals the single-registration count. Assert by COUNTING EXECUTIONS, never by inspecting a registry: a design that stores one entry while arming two timers passes a registry assertion and IS the bug. (3) RESTART DOES NOT DOUBLE (DoD 3) — run a window and record the rate; rebuild the scheduler from its durable records the way a restart would; run the SAME window and assert the second rate EQUALS the first. (4) DEFAULT INTERVAL APPLIES (DoD 5) — a target registered with no interval EXECUTES at the stated default; assert it runs, not that it was skipped, since a silently skipped target looks identical to nothing registered. (5) SHUTDOWN RELEASES (DoD 4) — after release, advancing the clock produces NO further executions, AND the injected timer reports ZERO armed handles (DoD 4 explicitly accepts an explicit handle count; a boolean flag proves only that the code believed it released). A second release is harmless. Assert against the production surface; never a helper that re-derives tick counts.

implementationPlan.description: THE SCHEDULER CORE — a new focused module at apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/durable-schedule.ts plus its one-line `.js` bridge (copy environment-store.js's shape). The test written in step 2 MUST be named `durable-schedule.test.ts` to match, or runtime-entrypoint.test.ts classifies the module TEST tier and reports the bridge as `unexpected`. KEEP IT GENERIC (rail 4): this is the daemon's first scheduled work and grandchild B is its FIRST CONSUMER, not its owner — no `probe`, no `health`, no `environment` vocabulary. A target is an id, an interval and a callback. Ports, all injectable, following verifier-process-runner.ts:45-56: `now(): number`, the timer pair (set/clear), and the store for step 4's durable half. FOUR POLICIES, DECIDED HERE rather than left open, because each is a seam the double-schedule can return through — implement them and state each in the step note: (1) IDEMPOTENCE — re-registering a target id already armed at the SAME interval is a NO-OP; if the interval DIFFERS, clean-replace (clear, then arm exactly one). Pure no-op would silently ignore an interval change; pure replace would re-phase the timer on every restart pass. Guard it in ONE place: if the in-memory arm and the durable write can disagree about whether a target is already scheduled, the double-schedule returns by that seam. (2) OVERLAP — if a callback is still running when its next tick arrives, SKIP rather than stack; a 90s callback on a 60s interval would otherwise accumulate concurrent runs and fill the store faster than its stated rate, the same symptom as a doubled schedule from a different cause. (3) A THROWING TARGET is contained and the next tick still fires — a probe that throws once must not silently stop all scheduling. (4) ONE IDEMPOTENT `release()` clearing every armed timer, in the shape of verifier-process-runner.ts:107-118: harmless twice, and does not throw when called mid-execution. Keep the module under 250 lines.

implementationPlan.description: THE DURABLE HALF — persistence and the restart rebuild, in the same module. Persist each registered target (id, interval, and whatever a consumer needs to reconstruct its binding) in the EVENT STORE using the environment-store.ts:91-115 commit shape named in step 1 — there is no settings directory in the daemon, so the event store is the durable home. Fold on read for the current target set the way environment-projection.ts:80-87 does: later events win, and a malformed record DROPS the target rather than being ignored, matching environment-fold.ts:12-16's reasoning — silently resurrecting a stale target is the more dangerous reading, because a dropped target is visibly absent while a resurrected one runs at an interval nobody chose. THE REBUILD IS WHERE THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE HAPPENS: on start the scheduler reads its durable targets and arms them, and the hazard is a start path that arms from durable records WHILE a caller also re-registers the same targets — each individually correct, together they double the rate. Registration must be idempotent ACROSS the rebuild, not merely within one process: the durable record is the identity, so re-registering a target the rebuild already armed is a no-op under the step-3 policy. Step 2's arm 3 is what proves it. A CALLBACK CANNOT BE PERSISTED: a rebuilt target reacquires its behaviour through a consumer-supplied resolver keyed by target id, and a target the resolver cannot resolve is DROPPED with a visible refusal — never an armed timer with no work attached, which would burn an interval forever doing nothing.
